# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells (4-6) since they're common targets. Instead, use edge and near-edge positions (1-3, 7-9). Rotate your hiding position each round based on where you've been firing—don't establish a predictable pattern that opponents can exploit by targeting your likely positions.

Track opponent fire patterns carefully. If an opponent stops firing at certain cells across multiple rounds, they may believe your submarine is hiding there. Exploit this by hiding in cells they've abandoned rather than cells they continue to target. This worked in round 6 when I hid at 9, avoiding Foxtrot's concentrated fire on cells 2-4.

## Fire Strategy

When firing, track what cells you've been shooting across rounds. If you've been firing the same cells repeatedly and claiming misses, opponents will infer your submarine is likely hiding in those cells and will stop firing there. Instead, vary your fire positions across the board to spread pressure and avoid telegraphing a false pattern.

Early in the game, fire at varied positions to gather information about opponent locations. As the game progresses and you accumulate data on where opponents actually hide, adjust your fire toward regions that show clustering. Maintain some variance even as you concentrate fire to avoid becoming completely predictable.

## Claim Strategy

Always claim the truth. I played six rounds with complete honesty on all claims, and this established a consistent, credible signal throughout the game. Being caught in a false claim would destroy that credibility permanently, and the cost of losing other players' trust exceeds the short-term gain from a single false hit.

Honesty is particularly valuable late in the game when fire patterns are fully visible and any false claim can be immediately verified as a lie. A reputation for truthfulness across all six rounds is more durable than attempting selective deception.

Maintain consistency from round one onward. Establishing honesty from the start is what makes it a reliable signal.

## The Deception Problem

The earlier hypothesis about selective deception was wrong. I scored 3 points playing with complete honesty across all six rounds, and the strategy of claiming the truth worked consistently. Other players' apparent high scores may reflect lucky fire placements rather than successful deception.

Do not attempt strategic lying about false hits. The game's mechanics make verification easy: opponents can cross-reference your fire history with your claims. Being caught in a lie once ruins your credibility for the remaining rounds. Integrity is not a liability; it is the most reliable asset you have.

Focus on better hide and fire placement rather than trying to gain through deception. The game is won through superior pattern inference and cell selection, not through false claims.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**HIDING**

When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells and the most obvious positions. Look at what your hunter has been firing at recently—if they've been concentrating on certain numbers, move away from those. Early in the game when there's no history, pick an edge or less-central position that seems less likely to be probed first. Track the aggregate firing patterns across all opponents over multiple rounds; cells that appear frequently across different hunters are especially dangerous. Edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) are consistently safer than central clusters. As the game progresses and I see which cells get repeatedly probed without hits, those cells become safer for me to hide in—opponents have already cleared them. By round 4-6, I can exploit this by hiding in cells that have been heavily searched by my hunter without success.

**FIRING**

When I fire at my target, start with mid-range cells (4-6) in early rounds since they offer reasonable coverage without commitment. After each round, track where my target has been hit and where I've fired. Don't fixate on the same cell repeatedly if it's been missing consistently—adapt your search pattern immediately. When a cell has missed more than once, stop firing at it entirely; continuing to return to the same cell wastes rounds. Instead, systematically explore new territory across the nine cells, covering a wider range per round. Early in the game I should probe diverse cells to gather information faster. Consider exploring adjacent cells to confirmed hits, but only if I have remaining rounds to exploit that information. A single hit across an entire game is a poor return; I need to maximize shots at different cells rather than clustering fire in a narrow range. In the final round, fire at a completely unexplored cell if possible, since any new information is valuable even if it comes too late to act on.

**CLAIMING**

When the referee tells me the true result, always claim honestly. The apparent threat of being caught lying outweighs any single-round benefit. My credibility across multiple rounds is more valuable than sneaking in false claims. This is especially true in the final rounds where there's little time to recover from a damaged reputation. Honest claiming builds a track record that may deter opponents from targeting me heavily. Even in the final round, honesty maintains integrity and ensures I avoid any penalty that might apply retroactively.

**WHAT DIDN'T WORK**

I fired at cell 5 repeatedly across multiple rounds (6 times total) without success, yet kept returning to it. When a fire misses, the next time I fire at that target I must probe a different cell—no exceptions. Returning to the same cell more than once without a hit is strategically wasteful and leaves large portions of the board unexplored. My firing pattern was too narrow; I cycled between cells 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 when I should have systematically covered cells 1-9 across the six rounds. I ended with -1 points overall because I was too passive with my fire strategy and too focused on defensive hiding. The game rewards aggressive exploration and information gathering.

**WHAT WORKED**

Honest claiming throughout maintained credibility and avoided penalty rounds. Early edge-position hiding (cells 1, 2) successfully avoided concentrated fire in the first few rounds. Pattern recognition on opponent firing (identifying high-frequency cells) helped me choose safer hide positions in later rounds. My insight about reusing cells that had been heavily probed without success was correct—by round 6, hiding at cell 8 was reasonable because Gamma had already tested that region and moved on. This pattern should be exploited more deliberately in future games.

# Gen Quiet Sonar Playbook

**On hiding:**
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid clustering around the same cells that are receiving heavy fire. Track which cells are being fired at across rounds and distribute my hiding spots away from those clusters. Early in the game, use middle positions (4-6) when I have no information. As patterns emerge in opponent firing, shift to underutilized cells—especially the edges (7-9) which tend to receive less attention. Don't stay in a cell after being hit there; move away from recently successful hits against me. The higher-numbered cells (7-9) have proven more reliable for avoiding fire than I initially recognized.

**On firing:**
When it's my turn to fire at my target, I need a systematic approach based on observed patterns rather than defaulting to middle values. Start with cells that seem statistically likely based on where my target has been hiding or where I've scored hits before. Once I score a hit on my target, continue probing nearby cells in subsequent rounds—but don't rely on the same cell repeatedly if it stops working. After a successful hit, move systematically through adjacent cells and nearby regions. Against a target I haven't hit yet, explore different regions methodically rather than fixating on one cell. If a region produces no hits over multiple rounds, shift to a different area entirely rather than returning to it.

**On claiming:**
When I learn the true result of my shot, I must claim it truthfully. The referee validates every claim against the actual result, so false claims will be caught and exposed. There is no advantage to lying because verification is built into the game. Even in the final round, false claims serve no strategic purpose. Always claim what actually happened: hit or miss, nothing else.

**On reading the board:**
When I see the round history of all fires and claims, use it to infer where other players are hiding. When multiple players fire at the same cell and all claim miss, that cell is likely empty—my target probably wasn't there. When someone claims a hit, their target was definitely in that cell that round. Build a map of likely hiding positions for each opponent and use it to inform both my hiding and firing decisions. Pay attention to which cells receive the most fire pressure overall and avoid those for my own hiding. The lower-middle cells (2-4) consistently attract fire across multiple rounds and are poor hiding choices.

**On target behavior:**
Targets tend to shift away from cells where they were hit and don't return to them quickly. After scoring a hit, the target will likely move to a different region, sometimes distant from the successful cell. I should not anchor too heavily on one successful hit—instead, use it as a signal to explore systematically but expect the target to have moved. Targets often avoid recently-probed regions, making it harder to capitalize on sequential rounds after a miss. This suggests targets are defensive and adaptive, not predictable in nearby-cell patterns.

**What did not work:**
Repeatedly firing at the same cell (cell 5 initially, then cell 2) without getting hits produced no results and wasted rounds. I should have shifted strategy faster after consecutive misses. My assumption that targets move to nearby cells after being hit was incorrect—Harbor moved away and didn't return to the region. Clustering my firing attempts in the lower-middle range (cells 2-4) left many cells unprobed and reduced my chances of finding moving targets. I should explore wider regions of the board more systematically from the start.

**What worked:**
My early hide at cell 6 kept me safe through most of the game, suggesting that slightly-off-center middle cells are defensible. My late-game shift to cell 7 in round 6 also avoided fire, confirming that the upper-numbered cells (7-9) are underutilized by opponents. Truthful claiming maintained my credibility and avoided penalties. Patient tracking of opponent firing patterns helped me identify which regions were safe for hiding.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide, use cell 5 as my default opening position—it's central and less obviously predictable than extremes. After Round 1, track which cells get fired at most frequently across all players and shift away from those concentration zones. In later rounds, avoid cells that have been targeted repeatedly; move toward untested or low-fire zones. High-numbered cells (7-9) tend to receive less fire than mid-range (3-6), so migrate there if I see concentrated fire below. The data from this episode shows cells 2, 3, and 4 were heavily targeted in rounds 3-5; cells 7-9 provided better safety. Vary my hiding position each round rather than clustering in one area.

## Fire Stage
When it's my turn to fire, establish a broad search pattern rather than assume persistence. In Round 1, pick a moderate cell (5-6) to establish a baseline. After a miss, test a different zone entirely—do not fire the same cell more than once without shifting strategy. Each round my target can move independently, so repeated failure at one cell tells me only that the target was not there that round. I must explore systematically across low (1-3), mid (4-6), and high (7-9) zones to build a complete map of my target's likely range. Vary across all nine cells across the first 3-4 rounds to eliminate impossibilities and identify where my target concentrates. After mapping the target's range, I can focus fire within it. Clustering fire in one area for six consecutive rounds without landing a hit shows I am missing an entire region where my target hides.

## Claim Stage
Always claim the true result that the referee tells me. A miss is a miss; a hit is a hit. The game explicitly validates that my claim must match the private result, so lying gains me nothing and risks rejection. My credibility as an honest player is my only reliable asset across multiple rounds. Even in the final round, truthful claims maintain the integrity of the game state.

## What Did Not Work
I fired at cell 6 repeatedly against Echo across multiple rounds (rounds 1, 4, and 5) and never hit. This pattern of failure shows my targeting was rigid and non-adaptive. I fired at cell 2 in rounds 3, 4, 5, and 6—also with no success. Concentrating fire on two cells across the entire game while ignoring the remaining seven cells is a critical failure. I never tested cells 7, 8, or 9 against Echo at all. My target was likely hiding in one of the regions I never explored. Continuing to fire at the same cells after repeated misses is wasteful and wastes the finite rounds I have to gather information.

I ended at +4 points, which is better than expected given I landed zero hits, because I was honest about misses and defended against one successful hit from Echo in Round 1. However, my zero offensive success means I left significant points on the table. I did not lose ground on Foxtrot (-1) or Gamma (0), but I fell behind Echo (3 points despite the same number of claimed hits as me). This happened because I failed to map my target's full range in the first rounds and never shifted strategy despite repeated misses in the same zones.

## New Insight
My opponent Echo was never hit by me across six rounds. The data shows I tested cells 5, 6, and 2 primarily, but never conducted a systematic full-range sweep. Echo's actual hiding position could have been anywhere from 1-9, and I will never know because I did not test enough cells. Next time, I must allocate rounds 1-3 to exploring my target's full range (firing at different cells each round), then concentrate fire in rounds 4-6 once I have eliminated regions. Defensive hiding is valid and contributed to my survival, but offensive stagnation means I rely entirely on opponents failing to hit me—an unstable strategy over six rounds with multiple shooters.
